# Conclusion

## Summary of Results

This research evaluated CaddySense, which was designed to back up and support golf performance analysis and coaching for all kinds of different golfers. The system was mainly created to bridge a gap that was seen in current sports analytics tools, which usually only account for elite athletes. They are also heavily focused on machine learning models, or do not contain interpretability at user-specific levels. To overcome this gap, this project was built around a system that puts together performance metrics, rule-backed analytics, and conversational AI advice that gives the user personalized, transparent, and accessible coaching advice to help them get better at the game of golf. 

The methods approach that was seen back in Chapter 3 showed that there was a layer of design that is able to separate data storage, evaluation based on certain metrics, and generative reasoning as a whole. This design of the tool was intentional, as it makes sure to balance interpretability and flexibility, but still maintains strong ethical implications, such as privacy preservation and giving the user full control. Instead of functioning as more of a predictive engine, CaddySense is seen more as a decision-backed system that is able to translate personalized performance data into more meaningful, explainable recommendations. 

The experimental evaluation, as seen in Chapter 4, examined more of the system behavior itself rather than predictive accuracy. This difference is important because the system's overall goal is not to predict performance outcomes, but to provide the user with more reliable, interpretable, and metric-backed advice. The evaluation was designed around specific research questions that looked into consistency, metric grounding, rule following, skill-level adaptation, and transparency under situations where the system may not have all the information. 

The results from these experimental questions overall clearly showed that CaddySense as a system successfully achieved its goals that were predetermined. The rule-backed layer showed full signs of consistency, which overall ensures that identical inputs given to the system would always produce the same classification, as well as the same findings in the weakness of the players. This is important for allowing the user to trust the system, as it proves that the system is predictable and reproducible. 
	
To add to consistency, CaddySense also demonstrated an impressive showing in grounding AI-generated advice in actionable performance metrics. Most of the responses successfully used and referenced structured data such as greens-in-regulation percentages, putting consistency, and driving distance. This idea of grounded proves that the recommendations are not random, and are directly linked to the performance patterns of the user. 
	
The following rules are another strong area that the system handled well. CaddySense was able to follow the predetermined rules when giving the user their personal training plan, the duration that it lasts for, the actual output length of the response, and the overall organization of the practice plan. These rules were put into place to make sure that recommendations stayed realistic and able to be completed by recreational players. This truly allowed the system to generate advice in a way that is consistent and also reduced the risk of overkill with complex or impractical advice that the user would not be able to take full advantage of. 
	
The results from experimentation also showed that the system was able to adapt its given feedback based on the specific golfer's skill level. Beginner golfers were given more simplified advice, while on the other end, advanced golfers were given more in-depth, detailed recommendations. This ability that the system uses is crucial for keeping up with the different skill levels of players using CaddySense.
	
At the end of the evaluation, CaddySense showed how it handles missing or incomplete data. Instead of giving the user false information or advice that is not backed up by metrics that do not exist, the system showed consistent adjustments in these cases and successfully gave the user recommendations using the metrics that they did provide for the system. This is another important aspect that makes the system more well-rounded, as the system is limited to its own knowledge instead of generating false claims that would essentially confuse or mislead the user. 
	
Aside from these strengths, the testing stage also brought up some limitations and trade-offs. The nature of the rule-backed layer, even though it is interpretable, can lead to certain situations where the system is unable to fully understand small performance variations. To add to this, even though rule-backed generation offers safety and ease of use, it can also capture the depth that generation recommendations achieve. 
	
Overall, the results show that CaddySense can truly demonstrate a successful AI coaching system that can be interpretable, transparent, and still follow ethical implications. The system opens a door for future research and further implementation and deployment in the world of AI-backed sports coaching. 

## Future Work

Since this research successfully proves a strong functional foundation of a strong system, there are many different directions for future work that could add to and extend the abilities of CaddySense. One of the biggest areas is the implementation of further performance tracking. The current system looks into performance based on session-level metrics, but it does not yet model exactly how performance changes and evolves. Adding a time-series aspect would allow the system to show more useful trends, show exact improvement, and allow the system to then give the user more rounded advice. This would give the system a sense to change from a one-scenario evaluator to a more ongoing coaching assistant that can adapt as the user progresses in their golfing career. 

Another idea for future work is the inclusion of more real-world user data through field experimentation. Even though synthetic data is used in this sturdy showed strong validity and overall experimental control, but it also limits how the system could truly provide feedback to real-world users. If future research involves user studies with actual recreational golfers to look into usability, engagement, and effectiveness overall, these studies could potentially provide feedback on how these users are using AI-generated feedback in order to improve at golf. CaddySense could also be designed further to include more performance metrics and data resources. For example, adding shot tracking technology, or wearable sensors, or GPS course information would allow the AI to add a more detailed explanation to the user when knowing more about the context of the scenario. This would also allow CaddySense to give more effective and precise recommendations. An area of concern with these new features, however, would need to be carefully added to maintain the system’s ethical implications when dealing with privacy and accessibility.

Table: Ideas of different directions that CaddySense could go in, organized by functionality and impact.

| Future Direction           | Description                                      | Impact Level|
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| Time-Series Tracking       | Track performance across multiple rounds         | High        |
| Real User Testing          | Validate system with actual golfers              | High        |
| Sensor Usage               | Incorporate swing or wearable data               | Medium      |
| Mobile App                 | Improve accessibility and usability              | High        |
| Model adjustment           | Improve prompt structure and reasoning accuracy  | Medium      |

Another potential direction that can be taken further could deal with the rebuilding of the rules layer. The current rule-based approach gives the system a strong sense of interpretability; there could be more exploration into scoring systems that use metrics or other probability reasoning. This could upgrade the system to be able to handle edge cases and more detailed performance patterns, without giving up transparency. When looking into AI capability, as AI gets more and more involved in the world, the future versions of this system could point towards more engineering techniques or other frameworks that work to further improve the efficiency and quality of generated feedback. To add to this, adding machines for user feedback on advice could create a way for the system to essentially train itself as it runs over time, learning from its previous mistakes and advice given to the users. Upgrading the scale of CaddySense is another area of improvement in the future. The current system is built for local-only execution, which allows for a strong privacy feature, but also limits deployment on a larger scale. In the future, this could be something that is considered as a potential, keeping this area for privacy protection, but also allowing for an option to include cloud-based add-ons that keep the user in control, while also giving them more functionality. 
	
Lastly, CaddySense could be adopted to other sports outside of just golf. The main methodology, which is able to combine metrics, conduct evaluations of players, and use conversational AI, has room to explore outside of the game of golf. For example, similar systems could be designed for fitness coaching, rehab for recovering from injury, or other user performance-driven activities. These are all future directions that show value, but also prove that CaddySense is not just a system alone, but a start for something that can turn into something much larger and represent more for human-centered AI coaching tools.

## Future Ethical Implications

As AI systems continue to be used in everyday decision-making, it is clear and essential to consider some ethical implications of their overall design and usage. While this specific research showed examples of many clear ethical examples, it also brings up more that need to be carefully considered when working on this system in the future. One main ethical strength CaddySense was designed around was data privacy. Since this system runs only in a local environment, it ensures that the user data remains under the user’s control and is not sent to any third-party servers. This was intentionally designed to eliminate the risk of misusing data and giving anyone unauthorized access to it. It can also raise questions about how privacy, as a whole, should be balanced against how a more complex system would function in the future. If later versions use cloud-based features or other methods for external data access, addressing these privacy concerns will be far more difficult as the system becomes more complex.

Another crucial ethical concern is transparency. CaddySense is built to provide advice that is purely backed up by the user’s performance metrics. This gives the user a sense of transparency and truly helps users understand the reasoning in their recommendations, and this would then gain their trust. As AI systems will become more complex in the future, keeping this same level of transparency will become more difficult. Future work on CaddySense must make sure that increased implementation does not directly affect the user's understanding of the responses they receive from the output of the system. Bias is another ethical concern that will not simply disappear. The system in its current state may avoid examples of bias by keeping its focus on metrics rather than other data; it is still possible for this bias to come up through assumptions made by the system about metrics. For example, if some metrics are affected by certain playing conditions like rain, the system must not assume this for every user, as it may not be raining during other players’ rounds. Evaluating other methods of environmental considerations is another area that the system needs to have in order to avoid bias and stay fair to all users.

The use of AI generation in itself shows another ethical concern that is directly related to the reliability and the user influence of the system. Even with the use of stronger grounding methods, there is still a risk that the user may rely too heavily on AI-generated advice. This could lead to less thinking or improper use of the advice given to them. To avoid this, systems like this one should make sure to keep emphasizing that the advice given to the user is suggestions and not direct demands. This will encourage users to interpret them however they want to within themselves. Another issue that can arise has to do with accountability. In previous coaching models, advice is clearly given from a human coach. In AI systems, accountability might become less clear, especially when the advice given to the user is generated using rule logic and other models. Future research could explore different methods for making sure to keep this accountability, such as explanation tracking or other features, such as an option for direct user feedback. Accessibility is another key detail when it comes to ethical concerns. CaddySense was designed to be very accessible to all kinds of golfers, not just the elite-level players. Future states of this system must make sure that the added functionality will not create hurdles for some users, such as required equipment or technical complexity that will confuse and turn away users who have a hard time understanding the system. Keeping this sense of accountability is important for allowing the benefits of AI coaching to be used for all skill levels of golfers and not limited to a targeted group of them.

Lastly, there is a social impact ethical concern that is directly related to the role that AI plays in skill development. CaddySense, as it becomes stronger in the future, may have an effect on how players are leaning and practicing their skills. Even though this can give benefits, it can also raise questions about the balance between human judgment and other guidance. Making sure that AI systems are supporting human learning processes and not replacing them will always be a main concern as technology moves into the future. Since all of the ethical implications have now been brought to attention, some things can be said about them. Future versions of CaddySense have to make sure it is transparent and has user control as its main design. Evaluation should also keep in mind the potential bias and to be sure to avoid them. Communication should also be made sure to keep within the predetermined rules when it comes to the generation of AI advice. Collaboration, when it comes to technology, ethics, and other methods, should be used to ensure that the AI system is developed correctly and safely.

| Ethical Area       | Addressed in Current System | Remaining Concern                  | Recommendation                      |
|--------------------|-----------------------------|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Data Privacy       | Yes (local storage)         | Data loss                          | Add secure backup options           |
| Bias               | Partially                   | Limited dataset changes            | Expand testing                      |

| Accessibility      | Yes                         | Limited UI deployment              | Develop mobile interface            |

## Closing Remarks

The research project mainly focuses on how artificial intelligence could be used to look into sports coaching in a way that can prioritize interpretability and accessibility, while maintaining ethical implications. Through the way the system is built and evaluated, CaddySense demonstrated that it is possible to create an AI system that can combine a structured analysis with a conversational AI coach that produces meaningful and transparent coaching recommendations. Instead of focusing on predictive models or automation, this system emphasizes a human-centered design and supports decisions made from personal players’ metrics. This approach shows a shift in AI research that can go alongside human capabilities, and not replace them as a whole.

Even though the system still has some limitations, it also proves to have a strong start for future works and gives ideas for future systems in the world of AI sports analytics. The results from this research show that putting together logic and generative AI can, in fact, produce systems that are effective but still follow ethical implications. As AI grows and adapts as time passes, the concerns addressed in this project, transparency, user control, and reasoning that is backed up by metrics, make up a helpful tool instead of one that is a risk or dangerous to users. CaddySense as a whole makes a strong start in the direction of the AI sports coaching world and offers a taste of how AI can be used to support skill development that is both responsible, intelligent, and effective.
